title: Level 1 Final Assessment
quiz.0.question: How many native grape varieties does Italy have?
quiz.0.explanation: Italy has more than 350 registered native varieties, the greatest grape diversity of any country, and almost every region has its own local varieties.
quiz.1.question: What is the correct order of Italian wine classifications from highest to lowest?
quiz.1.options.0: DOC > DOCG > IGT > Vino da Tavola
quiz.1.options.1: DOCG > DOC > IGT > Vino da Tavola
quiz.1.options.2: IGT > DOC > DOCG > Vino da Tavola
quiz.1.options.3: DOCG > IGT > DOC > Vino da Tavola
quiz.1.explanation: The correct order: DOCG (the highest, with a government quality guarantee) > DOC (controlled designation of origin) > IGT (geographical indication) > Vino da Tavola (table wine).
quiz.2.question: What does the "G" in DOCG stand for?
quiz.2.explanation: G = Garantita (guaranteed), the Italian state's official endorsement of quality and the core difference between DOCG and DOC. Every bottle of DOCG carries an anti-counterfeiting seal (fascetta).
quiz.3.question: Which grape is Barolo DOCG made from?
quiz.3.explanation: Barolo DOCG must be made from 100% Nebbiolo; called the "king of wines", it is Italy's most age-worthy top red.
quiz.4.question: Barbaresco and Barolo are both made from Nebbiolo. What is the main difference?
quiz.4.options.0: Barbaresco adds Barbera for more fruit
quiz.4.options.1: Barolo needs at least 38 months of ageing, Barbaresco at least 26, with a more forward, elegant style
quiz.4.options.3: Barolo can only be made in odd-numbered years
quiz.4.explanation: Barolo needs at least 38 months of ageing (Riserva 62), Barbaresco at least 26 (Riserva 50). Barbaresco, the "queen of wines", opens earlier than Barolo and is relatively elegant and refined.
quiz.5.question: What is the main characteristic of the Barbera grape?
quiz.5.options.0: High tannin, low acidity, for long ageing
quiz.5.options.1: High acidity, low tannin, a fine everyday wine
quiz.5.options.2: The only grape that can make sparkling wine
quiz.5.explanation: Barbera is known for high acidity and low tannin and is Piemonte's most widely planted grape; its wines are approachable and fruity, one of Italy's most important everyday red grapes.
quiz.6.question: What is the legal minimum ageing for Brunello di Montalcino DOCG?
quiz.6.explanation: Brunello di Montalcino must be aged at least 5 years (including 2 in oak), and Riserva at least 6 — one of the longest ageing requirements of any Italian DOCG.
quiz.7.question: What is the official emblem of Chianti Classico DOCG?
quiz.7.explanation: The black rooster (Gallo Nero) is the official emblem of Chianti Classico, representing the traditional heart of Chianti. It is said to come from a medieval legend in which Florence and Siena fixed their border by when their roosters crowed.
quiz.8.question: Which grape is Prosecco (Italian sparkling wine) made from?
quiz.8.explanation: Prosecco is made from the Glera grape (at least 85%), with its top area around Conegliano-Valdobbiadene in Veneto, mostly by the Charmat method (second fermentation in tank).
quiz.9.question: What is the main winemaking feature of Amarone della Valpolicella?
quiz.9.options.0: Frozen grapes are used to concentrate sugar
quiz.9.options.1: Made by appassimento, drying grapes to concentrate sugar
quiz.9.options.2: Brandy is added to raise the alcohol
quiz.9.explanation: Amarone uses appassimento (drying): grapes are dried in ventilated rooms for several months to concentrate the sugar and then fermented to dryness, giving a rich red with a minimum of 14% alcohol (often 15% or more).
quiz.10.question: Which grape is Soave DOC mainly made from?
quiz.10.explanation: Soave is based on Garganega (at least 70%), from Veneto, one of Italy's most famous white wine areas, crisp with almond notes.
quiz.11.question: Franciacorta DOCG is called "Italy's Champagne" because of which method?
quiz.11.options.0: The Charmat method (second fermentation in tank)
quiz.11.options.1: The traditional method (Metodo Classico, second fermentation in bottle)
quiz.11.explanation: Franciacorta uses the same traditional method as Champagne (Metodo Classico), with second fermentation in bottle and at least 18 months on the lees (Riserva 60), reaching world-class sparkling wine quality.
quiz.12.question: In which region is Valtellina, and what is its main grape?
quiz.12.explanation: Valtellina is in Lombardy, near the Swiss border, growing Nebbiolo (locally Chiavennasca) on mountain terraces; its most famous wines include Sforzato di Valtellina (a rich red from dried grapes).
quiz.13.question: Where in Italy does Nero d'Avola mainly come from?
quiz.13.explanation: Nero d'Avola is Sicily's most important native red grape, known for black fruit, chocolate and warm spice, the signature of Sicilian red wine.
quiz.14.question: Where is Nerello Mascalese most famous?
quiz.14.explanation: Nerello Mascalese performs best around Mount Etna in Sicily, where volcanic soils give distinctive minerality and elegant acidity; likened to Italy's Pinot Noir, it is one of the most fashionable Italian grapes internationally in recent years.
quiz.15.question: Which of these is one of Italy's five great white grapes?
quiz.15.explanation: Verdicchio is an important Italian white grape, mainly from Marche, most famous as Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi DOC — crisp, with a bitter-almond finish.
quiz.16.question: At which level are "Super Tuscans" usually labelled?
quiz.16.explanation: Because they use non-traditional grapes such as Cabernet Sauvignon or non-standard blends that don't meet DOC/DOCG rules, Super Tuscans are usually labelled Toscana IGT (some now fall under DOCs such as Bolgheri). Yet their quality often surpasses many DOCG wines — the highest achievement of the IGT level.
quiz.17.question: What is Sassicaia's special place in the Italian classification system?
quiz.17.options.1: Italy's first DOC covering a single estate (Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC)
quiz.17.options.2: Italy's first IGT to win an international award
quiz.17.options.3: Italy's only DOC allowed to add foreign grapes
quiz.17.explanation: Sassicaia is Italy's first DOC covering a single estate, full name "Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC", promoted in 1994. It is the forerunner of the Super Tuscans, made mainly from Cabernet Sauvignon.
quiz.18.question: In Italian food and wine pairing, what principle is "What grows together, goes together"?
quiz.18.options.0: Vegetables and wine from the same farm match best
quiz.18.options.1: Food and wine from the same region fit naturally, so regional pairing is the most reliable
quiz.18.options.2: Wine should be matched with food of the same colour
quiz.18.options.3: Only DOCG wines can go with fine food
quiz.18.explanation: This principle stresses that food (ingredients) and wine from the same region naturally complement each other, such as Chianti with Tuscan tripe stew or Barolo with white truffle risotto. Italy's regional dishes and local wines are often the result of centuries of shared evolution.
quiz.19.question: What is the ideal grape for tomato-sauce dishes (such as pasta or pizza)?
quiz.19.explanation: The high acidity of tomato sauce needs an equally high-acid wine, and Sangiovese's natural high acidity is the best choice. Low-acid wines taste flat with tomato sauce, and high-tannin reds become more astringent against the tomato's acidity.
quiz.20.question: What is the most traditional wine with Gorgonzola blue cheese?
quiz.20.explanation: Rich, salty blue cheese and sweet wine form a complementary contrast; the gentle sweetness of Moscato d'Asti with Gorgonzola's salty savour is a perfect traditional Italian pairing, the sweetness softening the cheese's strong flavour.
quiz.21.question: What type of wine is Marsala?
quiz.21.options.2: A sweet sparkling wine from Veneto
quiz.21.explanation: Marsala is a fortified wine from Sicily, with spirit added to raise the alcohol; it comes dry, semi-sweet (semisecco) and sweet (dolce), and is widely used in cooking (such as chicken Marsala) and for drinking.
quiz.22.question: Sforzato (Sfursat) di Valtellina DOCG is made most like which wine?
quiz.22.explanation: Sforzato and Amarone are both made by appassimento (drying the grapes); the difference is that Sforzato uses Nebbiolo (Chiavennasca) in the mountains of Valtellina in Lombardy, with alcohol of at least about 14%, in a more elegant style than Amarone.
quiz.23.question: What is Italy's position in world wine production?
quiz.23.options.0: One of the world's largest producers, often vying with France for first place
quiz.23.options.2: A small producer, mainly for the home market
quiz.23.explanation: Italy is one of the world's largest wine producers, vying with France for first place year after year; it is also among the leading exporters, with the US, Germany and the UK as its main export markets.
quiz.24.question: Which description of Pinot Grigio is most accurate?
quiz.24.options.0: A native Italian grape grown only in Piemonte
quiz.24.options.1: An international grape originally from France, at its best in north-east Italy (Friuli, Trentino)
quiz.24.explanation: Pinot Grigio is the Italian name for France's Pinot Gris; it performs best in north-east Italy (Friuli Venezia Giulia, Trentino-Alto Adige), is Italy's biggest-exporting white grape and is known for crispness and minerality.

slides.1.title: 📚 Scope and Instructions
slides.1.content:
This assessment covers the core knowledge of all 11 Level 1 lessons, with 25 questions.

📊 Classification: DOCG / DOC / IGT / Vino da Tavola
🗺️ Main regions: Piemonte, Tuscany, Veneto, Sicily, Lombardy
🍇 Core grapes: the five great reds + the five great whites
🍽️ Food and wine: the regional principle, classic pairings
🍾 Special wines: Amarone, Franciacorta, Marsala, Sforzato

Suggested time: 30 minutes | Pass mark: 70 (at least 18 correct answers)
slides.2.title: 🎯 Level 1 Key Review
slides.2.points.0: 🍷 Italy is one of the world's largest wine producers, with 350+ native grapes
slides.2.points.1: 📊 Classification: DOCG (highest) > DOC > IGT > Vino da Tavola
slides.2.points.2: 🏔️ The Apennines run the length of the country; three climate zones: continental / Mediterranean / hot Mediterranean
slides.2.points.3: 🗺️ North (Piemonte, Veneto, Lombardy): high-quality reds and sparkling wines
slides.2.points.5: 🗺️ South + islands (Sicily, Sardinia): rich native grapes
slides.2.points.6: 👑 Nebbiolo → Barolo DOCG (the king) + Barbaresco DOCG (the queen)
slides.2.points.8: 💪 Barbera: high acid, low tannin, a fine everyday wine, Piemonte's mainstay
slides.2.points.9: 🌊 Veneto's three treasures: Amarone (appassimento) / Soave / Prosecco (Glera)
slides.2.points.11: 🥂 Franciacorta DOCG: traditional-method sparkling, Italy's Champagne
slides.2.points.13: 🍇 Five great reds: Nebbiolo / Sangiovese / Barbera / Montepulciano / Nero d'Avola
slides.2.points.14: 🤍 Five great whites: Pinot Grigio / Trebbiano / Garganega / Verdicchio / Vermentino
slides.2.points.15: 🍽️ The regional pairing principle: What grows together, goes together
slides.2.points.16: 🍕 Tomato sauce → high-acid Sangiovese; cream sauce → white wine
slides.2.points.17: 🧀 Gorgonzola blue cheese → sweet Moscato d'Asti
slides.2.points.18: 📜 Marsala = Sicilian fortified wine; Sforzato = Valtellina dried-grape Nebbiolo
slides.2.points.19: 🎓 Congratulations on completing Level 1! Ready for Level 2?
